steps.title: What is this game called?
steps.help: The title. It goes on the gallery card and nowhere else.

field.hint: e.g. A Peasant's Quest

steps.title: One line that makes somebody want to play it
steps.help: Not a summary — a hook. This is the line under the title, and it is usually the only thing anyone reads before deciding.
steps.value: Seven days, one road, no choice.
steps.described: Seven days, one road, no choice.

field.hint: e.g. Seven days, one road, no choice.
field.placeholder: Seven days, one road, no choice.

steps.title: Write the introduction
steps.help: These lines set the stage. The player presses enter between each one, so break them where you want a beat.
value: You are a peasant. You have worked your old friend's farm for twenty-five years.
One morning, as you cut barley in the low field, a host of the king's guard rides through the standing crop as though it were water.

value.text: They tell you the king has called every man between twenty-two and thirty-five to the Dark Mountain. You have seven days to reach Hagan's Castle.

steps.described: You are a peasant. You have worked your old fri… (+2 more)

field.hint: one line at a time; a blank line ends it
field.placeholder: One morning the king's riders come through the barley…

steps.title: Who does the player play?
steps.help: An entity marked `playable`. One person, authored once — backgrounds are how they turn out differently.

steps.title: Where do they wake up?
steps.help: The first place the player sees. Make it somewhere they know.

steps.title: How many creation points does the player get?
steps.help: Spent at character creation on stats you marked `customizable`. Zero is a fine answer: not every game wants the player deciding who they are.

field.hint: 0 or more

steps.title: Which backgrounds are on offer?
steps.help: Optional. A background is who the protagonist was before the story started — different stats, different kit, sometimes a flag that opens a door later.

field.hint: numbers separated by commas, or blank for none

steps.title: How much time is one tick?
steps.help: The pace of everything: travel, weather, hunger, the seven days you have left. Thirty minutes suits a game about a week-long journey; a game about one night wants less. Blank leaves it at thirty.

field.hint: 1 or more

steps.title: Which calendar runs the year?
steps.help: Days, seasons, and parts of the day. `mace.core` has one.

steps.title: What time does the game open at?
steps.help: In ticks from midnight on day one. Mid-morning reads well.

field.hint: 0 or more

steps.title: What season is it?
steps.help: A season your calendar defines.

field.hint: e.g. autumn

steps.title: Which region seeds the weather?
steps.help: Where the sky starts. Usually the region the player is in.

steps.title: Which pool means life?
steps.help: When it empties, the player is done. Name it whatever your world calls it — the engine has no opinion, and blank leaves it at `hitpoints`.

field.hint: e.g. hitpoints

steps.title: Which pool does fighting cost?
steps.help: Every move in combat is paid for out of this. Blank leaves it at `stamina`.

field.hint: e.g. stamina

steps.title: How is combat played by default?
steps.help: The player can override this. Pick what your game is about.

options.label: tactical — untimed, and loses none of the reading
auto — the engine plays both sides

steps.title: Does death end the playthrough?
steps.help: No sends the player to a scene instead, which is how a game about a journey survives one bad night on the road.

field.hint: y / n

steps.title: Which survival systems are on?
steps.help: Exposure and rest are what give the weather teeth. Hunger and thirst are off unless your game is about rations.

field.hint: numbers separated by commas, or blank for none

options.label: exposure — the weather takes something out of you
rest — you have to stop, and stopping costs time

steps.title: How does money work?
steps.help: `simple` is enough for a story game: an item is worth its value and a shop is a scene you write. `market` runs the whole thing — a place is cheap because it grows the stuff, and closing a road makes it dear somewhere else.
steps.described: market — shelves, scarcity, and trade along the roads

options.label: simple — a price is an item's value, and shops are scenes
market — shelves, scarcity, and trade along the roads

steps.title: What is trade paid in?
steps.help: Only needed for a `market` economy, which has to settle a price the engine works out in something the player carries. Gold, ration chits, whatever your world spends.

steps.title: How hard is it, roughly?
steps.help: A label for the gallery. It changes nothing in the engine.

steps.title: Which quests start with the game?
steps.help: Quests not listed here have to be started by a scene. A quest in neither place is one nobody will ever see.

field.hint: numbers separated by commas, or blank for none

steps.title: What does winning mean?
steps.help: Checked after every action. A game with no win conditions and no quests cannot be won, which the validator will tell you.

field.hint: built one question at a time

steps.title: What does losing mean?
steps.help: Usually the vital pool running out, and often a deadline as well. Both can be true at once.
steps.described: The King's Summons has failed and `player.pools.hitpoints.current <= 0` is true

field.hint: built one question at a time

steps.title: Which scene plays when they win?
steps.help: The last thing anybody reads. Worth writing properly.

steps.title: What is this place called?
steps.help: What the player reads at the top of the screen.

field.hint: e.g. The Old Bridge

steps.title: What does it look like?
steps.help: One line is enough. Write more than one and you can make them conditional later — the bridge at night, the bridge in rain.
value: Six houses, a well, and more geese than people. The barley stands unfinished in the low field.
steps.described: Six houses, a well, and more geese than people.…

field.hint: one line at a time; a blank line ends it
field.placeholder: A stone span over black water, and moss on everything.

steps.title: Which region is it in?
steps.help: Regions are what the weather happens to. A place with no region gets the world's default sky.

steps.title: Is it indoors?
steps.help: Indoors means the weather cannot reach you. It still exists.

field.hint: y / n

steps.title: Can the player rest here?
steps.help: A game with nowhere safe is a game where the player can never recover, which is a decision rather than an oversight.

field.hint: y / n

steps.title: Who and what is here?
steps.help: Anything that should be standing here when the game begins.

field.hint: numbers separated by commas, or blank for none

steps.title: What can the player do here?
steps.help: Scenes offered as options on arrival. Anything a person here carries is offered too, so this is for the place itself.

field.hint: numbers separated by commas, or blank for none

steps.title: Does anything happen the moment they walk in?
steps.help: A scene that plays before the player is offered anything.

steps.title: Which encounter table does this place roll?
steps.help: Most places roll nothing. Roads are where the danger lives.

steps.title: Where can you go from here?
steps.help: Exits are how the map is drawn. A place with none is a place the player can walk into and never leave.

field.hint: add exits one at a time

steps.title: By which road?
steps.help: Leave it blank and the loader makes a one-tick road, which is fine for a door between two rooms and wrong for a day's walk.

steps.title: What should the option say?
steps.help: Blank gives you `Travel to <place>`.

field.hint: e.g. Take the north road

steps.title: Is it ever closed?
steps.help: Leave it empty and the way is always open.

field.hint: built one question at a time

steps.title: Where does it sit on the map?
steps.help: Only for the map view. Leave it blank and the layout works itself out from the routes.

field.hint: `x y` — or leave it blank and let the map lay itself out
